claim: Deletion of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain eliminates an inhibitory function of the domain and leads to uncontrolled and accelerated mRNA decapping by a constitutively activated and opportunistic Dcp2.
source: These results indicate that deletion of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain eliminates an inhibitory function of the domain and leads to uncontrolled and accelerated mRNA decapping by a constitutively activated and opportunistic Dcp2.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of down-regulated transcripts in dcp2-N245 cells.

claim: The observed up-regulation of transcripts in dcp2-N245 cells originates from a deficiency in mRNA decapping caused by loss of a positive regulatory function.
source: Evidence for positive regulation of the decapping enzyme is provided by the observation that elimination of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain also caused up-regulation of hundreds of specific transcripts. As this group of transcripts also exhibited concordant up-regulation in decapping-deficient cells (Figure 1B), it is likely that the observed up-regulation originates from a deficiency in mRNA decapping caused by loss of a positive regulatory function.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of up-regulated transcripts in dcp2-N245 cells.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Dcp2 encodes important regulatory activities.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that the C-terminal domain of Dcp2 encodes important regulatory activities and that loss of these regulatory activities can have direct consequences on decapping of hundreds of specific mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic experiments presented in the study.

claim: Loss of the regulatory activities of the Dcp2 C-terminal domain can have direct consequences on decapping of hundreds of specific mRNAs.

claim: Over the past decade mechanistic investigations of mRNA decapping regulation have largely been focused on the 245-amino acid N-terminal domain of Dcp2.
source: Over the past decade mechanistic investigations of mRNA decapping regulation have largely been focused on the 245-amino acid N-terminal domain of Dcp2, with essentially all biochemical and structural studies using this C-terminally truncated fragment (Mugridge et al., 2016; Borja et al., 2011; Floor et al., 2010; She et al., 2008; Deshmukh et al., 2008; She et al., 2006; Wurm et al., 2017; Wurm et al., 2016; Charenton et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Dcp2 N-terminal fragment binds to Dcp1, but lacks the binding sites for most decapping activators, including Pat1, Edc3, and Upf1.
source: This Dcp2 fragment binds to Dcp1, but lacks the binding sites for most decapping activators, including Pat1, Edc3, and Upf1 (He and Jacobson, 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of Dcp2 encodes a constitutively active decapping enzyme in vivo that can target a variety of mRNAs including those that normally use or do not use decapping-dependent mechanisms in their degradation.
source: Our genetic experiments here reveal that this N-terminal fragment of Dcp2 encodes a constitutively active decapping enzyme in vivo that can target a variety of mRNAs including those that normally use or do not use decapping-dependent mechanisms in their degradation (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is based on the genetic experiments presented in the study.

claim: Current models of mRNA decapping regulation based on the Dcp2 N-terminal domain may be informative with respect to the catalytic step of decapping, but most likely do not reflect complex aspects of mRNA decapping regulation in vivo such as substrate selection and decapping enzyme activation.
source: Accordingly, current models of mRNA decapping regulation based on the Dcp2 N-terminal domain may be informative with respect to the catalytic step of decapping, but most likely do not reflect complex aspects of mRNA decapping regulation in vivo such as substrate selection and decapping enzyme activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the genetic experiments presented in the study.

claim: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 have long been considered as general mRNA decapping activators.
source: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 have long been considered as general mRNA decapping activators and their functions are usually thought to be required for decapping of most wild-type mRNAs (Parker, 2012; Coller and Parker, 2004; Fischer and Weis, 2002; Coller et al., 2001; Bouveret et al., 2000; Tharun and Parker, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are only required for decapping of a subset of transcripts in yeast cells.
source: Contrary to this expectation, our expression profiling experiments revealed that Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are only required for decapping of a subset of transcripts in yeast cells and suggested that these factors have highly specific functions in controlling mRNA decapping (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling experiments presented in the study.

claim: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 have highly specific functions in controlling mRNA decapping.
source: Contrary to this expectation, our expression profiling experiments revealed that Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are only required for decapping of a subset of transcripts in yeast cells and suggested that these factors have highly specific functions in controlling mRNA decapping (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling experiments presented in the study.

claim: Pat1 and Lsm1 probably function as a Pat1-Lsm1-7 complex to target the same set of transcripts.
source: Consistent with strong in vivo physical interaction and shared in vitro RNA binding properties (Wu et al., 2014; Sharif and Conti, 2013; Bouveret et al., 2000; Chowdhury et al., 2007), our results indicate that Pat1 and Lsm1 function together (probably as a Pat1-Lsm1-7 complex) to target the same set of transcripts (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the expression profiling experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Decapping of individual mRNAs likely has different functional requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.
source: The partial overlap between transcripts commonly targeted by Pat1 and Lsm1 and those targeted by Dhh1 strongly indicates that these three decapping activators have distinct functions in mRNA decapping regulation and that decapping of individual mRNAs likely has different functional requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the partial overlap of targeted transcripts.

claim: mRNA decapping is a multi-step process.
source: Accordingly, our observation that decapping of individual mRNAs can have different requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 suggests that mRNA decapping is a multi-step process and that Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are likely to function at different steps of the decapping pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the different requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.

claim: Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are likely to function at different steps of the decapping pathway.
source: Accordingly, our observation that decapping of individual mRNAs can have different requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 suggests that mRNA decapping is a multi-step process and that Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 are likely to function at different steps of the decapping pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the different requirements for Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.

claim: Dhh1 may promote deadenylation.
source: Given the genetic and physical interactions between Dhh1 and the Not1-Ccr4 deadenylase complex (Chen et al., 2014; Rouya et al., 2014; Maillet and Collart, 2002; Hata et al., 1998; Ozgur et al., 2015; Mathys et al., 2014), and the physical interaction between Pat1 and Dcp2 (Charenton et al., 2017; He and Jacobson, 2015a), one possibility is that Dhh1 promotes deadenylation and that Pat1 and Lsm1 recruit the decapping enzyme.
evidence: This is a speculation based on genetic and physical interactions and supported by citations.

claim: Pat1 and Lsm1 may recruit the decapping enzyme.
source: Given the genetic and physical interactions between Dhh1 and the Not1-Ccr4 deadenylase complex (Chen et al., 2014; Rouya et al., 2014; Maillet and Collart, 2002; Hata et al., 1998; Ozgur et al., 2015; Mathys et al., 2014), and the physical interaction between Pat1 and Dcp2 (Charenton et al., 2017; He and Jacobson, 2015a), one possibility is that Dhh1 promotes deadenylation and that Pat1 and Lsm1 recruit the decapping enzyme.
evidence: This is a speculation based on genetic and physical interactions and supported by citations.

claim: Pat1 and Lsm1 may control a step after decapping, that is 5' to 3' exonucleolytic digestion.
source: In addition, since Pat1 and Lsm1, but not Dhh1, also interact with Xrn1 (Charenton et al., 2017), the former two factors may also control a step after decapping, that is 5' to 3' exonucleolytic digestion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the interaction with Xrn1 and supported by a citation.

claim: The functions of Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 in regulating decapping are probably linked to mRNA translation.
source: These observations indicate that the functions of Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 in regulating decapping are probably linked to mRNA translation, a conclusion consistent with a recent study linking Dhh1 function in mRNA decay to translation elongation through codon optimality (Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the translation properties of targeted transcripts and supported by a citation.

claim: The identity and distribution of non-optimal codons in an mRNA may influence the targeting specificity by Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.
source: Hence, the identity and distribution of non-optimal codons in an mRNA may influence the targeting specificity by Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that average codon optimality does not correlate well with Dhh1 requirement.

claim: The MFA2 mRNA is regulated by Pat1 and Lsm1, but not by Dhh1.
source: Both of these transcripts are in the datasets presented here and our results show that the MFA2 mRNA is regulated by Pat1 and Lsm1, but not by Dhh1, and that the PGK1 mRNA is not regulated by any of the three factors.
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling data presented in the study.

claim: The PGK1 mRNA is not regulated by Pat1, Lsm1, or Dhh1.

evidence: This is based on the expression profiling data presented in the study.

claim: It is difficult to justify models in which Dhh1 has a direct role in decapping of MFA2 and PGK1 reporter mRNAs.
source: Most importantly, since both reporter mRNAs are not regulated by Dhh1 it becomes difficult to justify models in which Dhh1 has a direct role in decapping of these transcripts (Coller and Parker, 2005; Fischer and Weis, 2002; Coller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that these reporter mRNAs are not regulated by Dhh1.

claim: Eliminating the functions of Pat1, Lsm1, or Dhh1 can have severe consequences for global mRNA accumulation.
source: Our expression profiling experiments revealed that, in addition to targeting specific mRNAs for decapping, Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 also have indirect roles in controlling mRNA expression in yeast and that eliminating the functions of any of these three factors can have severe consequences for global mRNA accumulation.
evidence: This is based on the expression profiling experiments presented in the study.

claim: Transcripts from the Down-o-d and Down-a-pld subgroups are sensitive to loss of both the regulatory and catalytic activities of mRNA decapping.
source: Collectively, these observations indicate that transcripts from the Down-o-d and Down-a-pld subgroups are sensitive to loss of both the regulatory and catalytic activities of mRNA decapping and argue that they are indirectly controlled by the status of general decapping activity in yeast cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the concordant down-regulation pattern.

claim: Transcripts from the Down-o-d and Down-a-pld subgroups are indirectly controlled by the status of general decapping activity in yeast cells.

claim: The susceptibility of transcripts from the Down-o-d and Down-a-pld subgroups to the loss of Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 functions is likely to be dictated by their unique properties in translation.
source: These observations suggest that the susceptibility of these transcripts to the loss of Pat1, Lsm1, and Dhh1 functions is likely to be dictated by their unique properties in translation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the translation properties of these transcripts.

evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation of more efficient NMD in dhh1∆ cells and supported by citations.

evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that these transcripts are not typical decapping substrates.

evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of indirect control.

evidence: This is based on the expression profiling data showing up-regulated transcripts.
